entities.name: Aratus of Sicyon
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Aratus of Sicyon (c. 271–212 BCE) was a pivotal figure in Hellenistic Greece, an architect of the Achaean League's expansion and a persistent opponent of Macedonian hegemony and Spartan resurgence. He served an unprecedented seventeen terms as strategos (general-in-chief) of the League, transforming a loose confederation of Peloponnesian city-states into a significant political and military power capable of challenging regional giants. His career spanned nearly five decades, marked by complex diplomacy, strategic military campaigns, and a relentless effort to secure the autonomy of Greek cities against external domination, particularly from the Antigonid dynasty of Macedon.

Exiled from Sicyon as a child after his father, Cleinias, was murdered by the tyrant Abantidas, Aratus returned in 251 BCE to liberate his native city, expelling the tyrant Nicocles and incorporating Sicyon into the nascent Achaean League. This act initiated his long political career within the League, culminating in his first election as strategos in 245 BCE. Over subsequent decades, Aratus masterminded the League's expansion, notably orchestrating the surprising annexation of Corinth in 243 BCE and Argos in 229 BCE, bringing much of the Peloponnese under Achaean influence. He led the League through major conflicts, including the Cleomenean War (229–222 BCE) against Sparta's reformist king Cleomenes III, and later the Social War (220–217 BCE) against the Aetolian League, often balancing Achaean independence against the necessity of Macedonian support.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Aratus of Sicyon significantly shaped the political landscape of Hellenistic Greece through his unparalleled leadership of the Achaean League, expanding its territory and influence across the Peloponnese. His complex diplomatic and military strategies, though ultimately leading to increased Macedonian involvement, established a robust federal structure and set precedents for Greek resistance against larger powers.
